extracted.intended_audience: educated general readership interested in mathematics, probability, and skeptical critique of pseudoscience
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and judge mathematical/paradoxical claims, empirical probability experiments, pedagogical proposals, and related heterodox writings — weighing demonstration, evidence, and method. Applicable to critical reading of 19th‑century and popular-science polemical texts about mathematics and science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for mathematical demonstration (not opinion or dogma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments about mathematical truth should rest on demonstration rather than on authority or mere opinion; contempt of demonstration is an intellectual fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: 'contempt of demonstration such as our paradoxers show' and 'the D in demonstration is the D in durability.' Use formal proof and demonstrative argument as the primary standard. Anti-patterns: replacing demonstration with appeals to personal belief, rhetorical force, or the mere popularity of an idea. Evaluate paradoxical claims by whether they contradict established demonstrations and, if so, whether the claimant supplies an explicit, valid refutation rather than mere assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of opinion must not supplant demonstrative standards
rubrics_metrics.description: While freedom of opinion and rejection of dogmatic authority are socially valuable, they should not lead to the rejection of demonstrative proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From: 'Freedom of opinion... whether contempt of demonstration such as our paradoxers show has augmented with the rejection of dogmatic authority.' Guidance: encourage open discussion but maintain that skepticism of authority should increase, not decrease, respect for demonstration. Do not conflate dissent from authority with justification to ignore mathematical demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical verification in probability requires large numbers of trials (law of large numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilistic predictions manifest in long-run frequencies; many trials are required to approach theoretical averages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Buffon's and others' experiments: e.g., in 2,048 sets the observed frequencies approached theoretical proportions (H ≈ 1/2, TH ≈ 1/4, ...). Principle: 'whatever can happen will happen if we make trials enough'; use large sample sizes for reliable empirical estimates. Scoring note: judge experiments by number of trials, closeness to theoretical expectation, and treatment of ambiguous results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buffon's-needle method as an empirical estimator for π
rubrics_metrics.description: A repeated-random-placement experiment (rod/wire on planked floor) can estimate π from the long-run fraction of intersections of seams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: fraction of trials in which a seam is intersected → equals (2 * length of rod) / (circumference of circle with plank breadth as diameter) → yields π. Examples and results from Ambrose Smith (3,204 trials gave π = 3.1553 or 3.1412 depending on contact treatment) and a pupil (600 trials gave π = 3.137). Guidance: perform many trials; decide and state how ambiguous contacts are handled (e.g., count half as intersection); report sample size and handling of borderline cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the gambler's fallacy; treat independent trials properly
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer that past streaks affect the probability of future independent events (e.g., believing 'red' must be due after many 'red' outcomes is mistaken).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: roulette behaviour (red/black) and the French lottery; observation that gamblers misapply notions like 'what has not happened for a long time must soon come.' Anti-pattern: basing predictions on the false notion that short-run deviations will 'self-correct' in the next trial. Evaluation: check independence assumptions and compute expected frequencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical principle: 'Tout est dans tout' / mastery of a small core
rubrics_metrics.description: Jacotot method principle: 'Tout est dans tout' — learn some part thoroughly and relate the rest to it; mastering a small, well-chosen body of propositions can facilitate broader learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'Tout est dans tout' and 'Apprendre quelque chose, et à y rapporter tout le reste.' Practical guidance: use focused memorization and well-chosen exemplar problems (the tract gives conic propositions and exercises). Anti-pattern: superficial breadth (crammed erudition) without deep hooks for later learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent registration and truthful representation for medical (or professional) practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: If regulating practice by registration, the register should show name, address, and asserted qualifications; practitioners must declare qualifications, provable qualifications should be proved, and false representation must be penalised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed elements proposed: register republished every six months; allow any description of qualification (diploma, private study, intuition) but require proof where possible; penalize asserting qualifications not in the register; make register inexpensive and accessible to patients; allow patients to demand and inspect the registered qualifications; make false representation bar recovery of fees and expose practitioners to fine/imprisonment. Use of register as evidence: medical witnesses should produce their register entry in court. These are procedural standards for protecting patients and improving public information; evaluate proposals by enforceability, transparency, and patient remedy mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical assessment of system-driven authors and confirmation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author organizes facts to fit a grand system, treat their claims with caution and cross-check authorities and direct evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the Higgins example: the author 'saw his system in the way the fact was presented to him by his authority.' Practical checks: consult independent experts, verify primary sources, and compare direct observation (e.g., the Indian officer's counterexample) against claimed universal correspondences. Anti-pattern: accepting broad historical or comparative claims because of the quantity of citations or an impressive index without checking for selective use of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of constrained linguistic exercises (pangs/pangrams) as attention devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises like Cabbala Alphabetica (sentences containing every letter once) are useful for securing attention to letters and spelling; useful in teaching orthography and observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: 'I, quartz pyx, who fling muck beds.' Guidance: include v and j treated as consonants; such constrained writing helps learners notice letter forms and frequency. Use as writing-copy exercises to ensure attention to every letter; consider suitability for intended learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical evaluation of implausible scientific explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary or ad-hoc mechanistic claims (e.g., friction causes magnetism; metaphysical numerology) demand skepticism and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Pope's 'Triumphal Chariot of Friction' claims that friction of the air causes magnetism and derives metaphysical attributes from geometric constructions. Guidance: check claims against established physics, seek empirical tests, and beware of grand metaphysical inferences drawn from tenuous mathematical constructions. Anti-pattern: accepting elaborate speculations because they are couched in mathematical language or carry impressive plates/subscriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, practical terminology in elementary texts (use conventional examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: In elementary expositions, prefer familiar, conventional terminology and concrete examples rather than awkward euphemisms which obscure understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sir John Lubbock preferred the singular 'probability' over 'probabilities'; he also avoided slang and used 'obverse'/'reverse' rather than 'head'/'tail' — but practical force of examples (race-horse name 'Bessy Bedlam') forced use of common terms. Guidance: favor clarity and commonly understood terminology in examples to aid reader comprehension; adapt examples when necessary but avoid pedantry that impairs accessibility.
